I edit reports for a living, and the habit I spend most of my time fighting is the long sentence. Not because long sentences are wrong. A good long sentence is efficient. The documents attached to this email, the client mentioned in the minutes, the people working on the project: each of those phrases is a shorter version of a whole clause, and English readers process them very quickly. The problem starts when the writer loses track of who is doing what. My favorite example came from a report I edited last year. It said: having reviewed the figures, the budget looked unrealistic. Read it again. The budget did not review anything. Somebody did, and that somebody has disappeared from the sentence. So my advice is simple. Use the short forms as much as you like, but before you send anything, check that the first noun after the comma is the person who did the action.

I have written legal opinions for international clients for twenty-five years, and I have changed my mind about one thing. We still write pursuant to, and subject to, and hereinafter, and some of that language is genuinely useful, because it is precise. What I stopped doing is starting with it. A client reading in a second language should not have to decode three subordinate clauses to find out whether the answer is yes or no. So every opinion we send now opens with two sentences in plain English: the question, and our answer. The long sentence comes after that, for the lawyers on the other side and for the judge, if it ever gets that far. Clients have told me it is the first time they have read one of our opinions to the end. It costs us nothing, and it has probably prevented more disputes than any clause I have ever drafted.
